fields.meta_title: Ecommerce Automation for Store Operations | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build ecommerce automation for your store: route paid orders to suppliers and hold risky ones for review, as code you own. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build Ecommerce Automation for the Work Behind Every Order
fields.hero_description: Create ecommerce automation that sends each paid order to its supplier and alerts your team when an order needs a person.
fields.features_subheading: Ecommerce automation takes the order-by-order steps that repeat all day. Pricing and product decisions stay with you.
fields.feature_1:
Starts on the store event you pick

Connects to Shopify, WooCommerce, or BigCommerce through their APIs. A paid order or a new customer signup starts each run, and every run is saved as a row you can search.
fields.feature_2:
Rules written the way you say them

Describe the condition in a sentence, such as no reorder email to anyone who bought in the last 30 days. Emergent writes the check and the skip, and you change either by prompting.
fields.feature_3:
Supplier and SKU records you own

Keeps your supplier table and SKU list in a database that belongs to you. Every workflow reads the same tables, and a new supplier means one new row, not a rebuilt workflow.
fields.feature_4:
Alerts where your team already works

Sends a Slack message or an email when a run needs a person to decide. A reminder goes out if nobody answers, and an unanswered hold escalates to the next name on the list.
fields.feature_5:
No task cap during a sale week

Runs every order through the same steps on the busiest day of your year. There is no task cap, and a flash sale with four times the usual orders never pauses a workflow halfway.
fields.feature_6:
Code in your own GitHub repo

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub repo on paid plans. Anyone with access can read every rule or add a carrier, and the app runs wherever the rest of your stack is hosted.

fields.tab_content_1:
Each paid order goes to the supplier who stocks it

Fernhill Home sells through Shopify and holds no stock. When an order is paid, the app splits its lines by supplier: order #10482 becomes a purchase order for Kilnworks and another for Northwind Textiles, each with the ship-to address. The tracking number a supplier enters is written back to the Shopify order.
fields.tab_content_2:
When a customer goes quiet for 90 days

Customers who have not ordered in 90 days get a winback email the next morning with COMEBACK10, a code for 10% off. The app reads the subscription field first and skips anyone who unsubscribed. Each send is logged on the customer's record, and an order placed with the code counts as won back.
fields.tab_content_3:
Hold the $500 order that ships somewhere new

Any paid order over $500 whose shipping address differs from the billing address stops before the warehouse queue. Dana Whitfield, the ops lead, gets a Slack direct message with both addresses and the customer's past orders. Release sends it to packing. Cancel closes it in Shopify and saves her reason.
fields.tab_content_4:
Margin per SKU after shipping, every Monday

Every Monday at 7:00 AM, the app pulls last week's Shopify orders and rolls them up by SKU. Each row carries units, revenue, product cost, and shipping. Margin is what is left after cost and shipping, as a share of revenue. Any SKU under 20% is flagged, and the report goes to Sam Ortega, the founder, by email.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to start ecommerce automation with one store event and one rule, then run it beside your manual process.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick one event and one rule
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Map every SKU to a supplier
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the jobs someone on your team repeats for every order or customer: forwarding orders, chasing tracking numbers, checking large orders, building the weekly numbers. Note how often each one happens and who does it today.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Choose one store event to start with, such as a paid order, and the rule that follows it. Write the rule with its numbers and names: which supplier, what amount, who gets the message, and what happens when nobody replies.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Put every SKU in one sheet with its supplier, the supplier's order inbox, and the unit cost. Workflows that route orders or report margin read from this table, and any SKU missing a supplier is flagged for you instead of guessed.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tell Emergent what starts the workflow and what each run should write, naming the people who decide. Emergent builds the workflow and its database tables with a dashboard on top, and you adjust any step by prompting again.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Point the app at a development store or replay last month's orders before it touches live ones. Compare each result, order by order, with what your team did by hand that day. Include a busy sale day in the replay to see the app handle a real peak.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Run it beside the manual process
fields.howto_step_6_des: Keep doing the work by hand for the first week while the app logs what it would have done. Every mismatch between the two becomes a change to the rule, and you switch over once a full week matches.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Build the second workflow on the data the first one already uses. The supplier table behind dropship routing is the table the Monday margin report reads, and each new workflow starts with less setup than the one before it.

truth.evidence: CAN-SPAM opt-out and 10 business days match the FTC guide; Shopify orders/paid and fulfillment tracking sourced; margins check: (3360-1260-588)/3360 = 45%, (2790-1550-899)/2790 = 12% ($341), 40%, 37%; $742 > $500.
